articles.title: Read the deal, not the ad

body.support:
A phone ad wants you to sign up. It puts the good bits in big print.

It uses two kinds of words:

- **Facts** you can check. *$35 a month.*
- **Opinions** you can't check. *Best network!*

The **small print** has the rules. Look for these catches:

1. **The price goes up.** *$35 for 6 months, then $55.*
2. **The speed drops.** Unlimited data might get slow.
3. **You're locked in.** You may have to pay to leave.

To compare two plans, work out the cost for **a whole year**. Then pick the one that suits you.
body.core:
A phone plan ad is a **persuasive text**. Its job is to get you to sign up, so it puts the best bits in big, bright print.

The ad mixes two kinds of language:

- **Facts** you can check: *$35 a month*, *40 GB*, *12-month contract*.
- **Opinions** you can't check: *best network*, *amazing value*, *you'll love it*.

The **small print** is where the conditions live. Look for three common catches:

1. **The price goes up.** *$35/month for the first 6 months, then $55.*
2. **The speed drops.** *Unlimited data* might slow right down after a set amount.
3. **You're locked in.** A **contract** can mean a fee if you leave early.

To compare two plans fairly, work out the **cost for a whole year**, not just one month. Then ask what you really get, what the catch is, and which plan suits the person who'll use it.
body.extend:
A phone plan ad is a **persuasive text**: everything in it is designed to make you sign up. The headline shows off the best features, and the conditions get pushed into the fine print.

The ad mixes **objective** language (*$35 a month*, *40 GB*) with **subjective** language (*best network*, *amazing value*). Only the objective claims can be checked. The subjective ones are there to create a feeling.

Three catches turn up again and again in the fine print:

1. **Starter prices**: a low price for a few months, then a higher one.
2. **Speed limits**: “unlimited” data that slows right down after a cap.
3. **Lock-in**: a contract with fees for leaving early.

A fair comparison works out the **total cost over twelve months**, checks what's included, and weighs it against the needs of the person using it.

caseStudies.title: The NBN speeds that weren't

body.support:
Internet companies sold plans with speeds like **“up to 100”**. Lots of people paid extra. But their internet could never go that fast.

The **ACCC** looks out for shoppers in Australia. It made the companies give money back. Telstra gave refunds to **42,000** people.

In 2022, a court made **Telstra, Optus and TPG** pay **$33.5 million** in fines. They agreed their ads were wrong.

The lesson: a number in an ad is a promise. Check what you really get.
body.core:
For years, internet companies sold home plans with speeds like **“up to 100”**. Lots of people paid extra for the fast speed. But many of their connections could never go that fast.

The **ACCC** is the government body that looks out for shoppers. In 2017 and 2018 it made Telstra, Optus, TPG and others offer fixes and money back. Telstra alone gave refunds to **42,000** people.

In 2022, a court ordered **Telstra, Optus and TPG** to pay **$33.5 million** in fines. The companies agreed that what they said about top speeds was false or misleading.

The lesson: a number in an ad is only a promise. Check what you will really get.
body.extend:
For years, internet companies sold home plans by their top speeds, such as **“up to 100 Mbps”**. Many customers paid more for the fast tiers, even though their connection could never reach those speeds.

The **ACCC**, the national consumer watchdog, stepped in during 2017 and 2018. Telstra, Optus, TPG and others agreed to offer fixes and refunds. Telstra's refunds alone went to about **42,000** customers.

In 2022 the Federal Court ordered **Telstra ($15 million), Optus ($13.5 million) and TPG ($5 million)** to pay fines totalling **$33.5 million**. The companies admitted their claims about top speeds were false or misleading. They had no good system for telling customers when those speeds couldn't be reached.

A number in an ad is a claim, not a promise. Smart readers ask: when is this actually true?

teacher.overview: Students read phone plan ads as persuasive texts: separating objective (fact) from subjective (opinion) language, finding the conditions in the small print, and comparing two plans by their 12-month cost. The case study is the ACCC's action over misleading NBN speed claims. The final task is a recommendation to a friend backed by facts.

teacher.answers:
**Ad:** 1 headline (opinion); 2 big price with a star; 3 price rises to $55 after 6 months; 4 speed slows after 40 GB; 5 12-month contract, exit fee; 6 deadline to rush you.

**Fact or opinion:** 40 GB — fact; best network — opinion; 12-month contract — fact; never want to switch — opinion; amazing value — opinion; price rises to $55 — fact.

**Showdown:** Plan A 12 months = 6 × $35 + 6 × $55 = **$540**. Plan B = 12 × $40 = **$480**. Plan A: 40 GB then slow; catch = price rise, lock-in. Plan B: 30 GB, no contract, rollover. **For Jaz** (25 GB, might move in 8 months): Plan B — cheaper over a year, enough data, and no exit fee when Jaz moves.

realityCheck: **Money can be sensitive.** Some students don't have a plan of their own, or their family is under financial stress. Keep it about the fictional Jaz, and don't ask students to share their own bills.
**The maths is light but real.** The 12-month cost trips up some students. Model one calculation and allow calculators: it's literacy, not a maths test.
**Real plans change monthly.** If you use real ads for the hook or Level Up, screenshot them the week you teach.
**Most engaging bit:** the hook vote and the reveal that the “cheaper” plan costs $60 more. Leave time for that discussion.
**Timing:** three 50-minute lessons is realistic. If you only have two, set the Level Up for home and do the case study as a whole-class read.
